text:
Times Exclusive … A Billionaire Wanted a Trump Pardon. His Family Gave Alina Habba a $50 Million Deal.

Listen · 7:27 min
20OCT2026 
By Tyler Pager
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/rLdY6V10oL
Julio Reporting from Washington

Herrera Velutini, a prominent Venezuelan, was seeking clemency. He got it not long after his daughter gave Ms. Habba, a lawyer close to President Trump, an extraordinarily lucrative job.

Julio Herrera Velutini really wanted a pardon.

A billionaire banker from a prominent Venezuelan family, Mr. Herrera faced felony bribery charges in the United States and struck an unusually lenient plea deal in August 2025 for a misdemeanor campaign finance violation. But he felt that reduced charge was still a stain on his record.

So Mr. Herrera deployed his lawyer, Christopher M. Kise, the former Florida solicitor general who was on Mr. Trump’s personal legal team, to help with a plea for clemency. His 27-year-old daughter, Isabela Herrera, who is an American citizen, donated $3.5 million to a super PAC tied to Mr. Trump. But as of last fall, the pardon remained elusive.

Then the Herrera family hired Alina Habba, who had been one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and at the time was an adviser at the Justice Department. They offered her $10 million a year for four years along with a range of bonuses. In total, including bonuses, she was guaranteed more than $50 million over four years, according to interviews and documents obtained by The New York Times.

Under the agreement, Ms. Habba would become general counsel at Concord Partners, a company that Ms. Herrera set up in late October 2025 in Florida. The company has no public profile and its business remains unclear even to some people associated with the Herrera business empire. Ms. Habba finalized her deal days after the company was registered.

At the time, Ms. Habba was also a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. She had an office at the Justice Department and a protective detail from the U.S. Marshals, a holdover from her time serving as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

She formally began her work for Concord Partners on Jan. 1. Weeks later, Mr. Trump granted Mr. Herrera a full and unconditional pardon.

The sequence of events raises questions about how Mr. Herrera secured the pardon and who might have helped him. People familiar with Ms. Habba’s contract said they believed that she was brought in to help with Mr. Herrera’s push for a pardon and expressed surprise at the scale of the compensation.

Ms. Habba denied any role in the pardon.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she said in a statement.

Ms. Habba was a special government employee at the time, which allows individuals to work for the federal government for up to 130 days and maintain outside employment with conflict-of-interest restrictions.

She declined to discuss her work for Concord.

Ms. Herrera and Mr. Herrera did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did their companies. In a statement, the Justice Department said Ms. Habba did not speak to anyone about a pardon.

A White House official said that Ms. Habba had nothing to do with the pardon and that the administration follows a pardon review process that includes the White House Counsel’s Office and the Justice Department.

In Mr. Trump’s second term, a pardon industry has sprouted up, with wealthy criminals paying well-connected lawyers, fixers and lobbyists to appeal to the administration and its allies in an effort to secure pardons. Many pardon seekers have come to the conclusion that supporting Mr. Trump and his political agenda is the fastest way to secure clemency.

Some people looking for pardons have reported paying hundreds of thousands of dollars or even $1 million to hire people promising access to the president or influence over the pardon process.

For Ms. Habba, the job from the Herrera family came at a pivotal point in her life and career.

She resigned in December 2025 as U.S. attorney in New Jersey after a panel of federal judges ruled that her appointment by Mr. Trump had been carried out unlawfully. Her second marriage was also falling apart.

The arrangement with the Herreras provided her with a new level of financial security. She also found new love. Shortly after the pardon was issued, Ms. Habba started dating Turhan Mildon, a Turkish investor.

They were married last month in a lavish ceremony in New York. The guest list included Attorney General Todd Blanche; the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel; and Will Scharf, the White House counsel.

The couple is now engaged in high-profile feud with Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally. Ms. Habba has accused Mr. Grenell of misallocating a donation from her husband to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which Mr. Grenell was running at the time. Mr. Grenell has denied her accusations, calling them absurd.

Ms. Habba brought those accusations directly to Mr. Trump, who directed Mr. Scharf to investigate them. The Times has previously reported that the investigation centers on a bank transfer from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company.

Mr. Herrera, who also has Italian citizenship, is a member of the Herrera family, a banking, real estate and fashion dynasty that dates back to the 14th century. The family owns estates and castles in Caracas, Venezuela; the Canary Islands; Spain; and Germany.

Mr. Herrera founded a bank based in Puerto Rico in 2008.

In August 2022, he was charged for his role in a scheme to bribe Gov. Wanda Vázquez of Puerto Rico to dismiss a regulator who was investigating the bank. Mr. Herrera, Ms. Vázquez and a former F.B.I. agent who had worked as a consultant for Mr. Herrera all pleaded not guilty to felony charges.

Mr. Kise, Mr. Herrera’s lawyer, helped negotiate a deal with the Justice Department under which Mr. Herrera pleaded guilty in August 2025 to a single misdemeanor campaign finance charge. Ms. Vázquez and the former F.B.I. agent also pleaded guilty to misdemeanors, disappointing career prosecutors who had pushed for harsher sentences.

All three were pardoned by Mr. Trump at the same time, shortly before they were scheduled to be sentenced for the misdemeanor charges.

In July, Banvelca, the Herreras’ family office since 1781, announced that Ms. Herrera, a member of the eighth generation and the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, was assuming leadership of the company. Neither the news release nor her bio on the company’s website makes any mention of Concord Partners, the vehicle employing Ms. Habba, who now goes by Mrs. Mildon.

Kenneth P. Vogel contributed to this report.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Julio Herrera Velutini in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in August 2022, after being charged for his role in a scheme to bribe the territory’s governor, Wanda Vázquez, to dismiss a regulator who was investigating his bank.

Credit...Carlos Giusti/GFR Media, via Imago

text:
Inflation Is Bullshit

Every earnings call sounds the same: “inflationary pressures,” “rising input costs,” “challenging environment.” Then they announce record profits.

Look at the numbers. S&P 500 companies posted a 15.7% net profit margin in Q2 2026, the highest since FactSet started tracking in 2009. That’s the fourth record quarter in a row. The long-run average since 1946 is about 6 cents of profit per dollar of sales. Today it’s more than double that.

If costs were really squeezing these companies, margins would shrink. They’re expanding. That means prices are rising faster than costs. That isn’t inflation happening to corporations. It’s corporations happening to you.

This isn’t a fringe theory. The Groundwork Collaborative found corporate profits drove 53% of price growth in mid-2023, compared with about 11% over the previous four decades. The IMF found profits accounted for 45% of eurozone inflation in 2022.

Here’s how it works. A shock hits: a pandemic, a war, an oil spike. Everyone expects prices to rise. So companies raise them, and then raise them more than their costs justify, because “inflation” gives them cover. In markets with three or four big players, no one undercuts anyone. Why would they?

Meanwhile the same companies lay people off, offshore jobs, and buy back their own stock. Workers get told to tighten their belts. Shareholders get a record quarter.

And the “solution” we’re offered? The Fed raising interest rates, which means higher mortgage, car, and credit card payments for regular people, and slower hiring. We punish workers for a problem created in the boardroom.

Stop calling it inflation. Call it what it is: pricing power, consolidation, and greed. Start asking why we let industries consolidate to the point where competition stopped working.

#Greedflation

text:
Black Day for Baseball: White Sox Players Indicted For Throwing The World Series (20 October 1920)

The World Series of 1919 pitted the Chicago White Sox vs the Cincinnati Reds; the Sox were favored to win. Team owner Charles Comiskey was disliked by many players for underpaying them, opening the door for New York gambler Arnold Rothstein to offer money for players to lose games intentionally. Many noticed that a lot of money was being bet against Chicago raising alarm bells for many sports writers and others. The games were watched carefully to see if anything unusual was going on. By Game 5, those who were involved got angry they were not being paid and thus the Sox won Games 6 and 7. However, the gamblers made threats and Game 8 was lost to the Reds. The main conspirators received $5,000 while Chick Grandil, who initiated the scheme with Rothstein, got $35,000.

Rumors swirled that the game had been fixed and newspaper stories detailed corruption in other ball clubs leading to a grand jury being convened to investigate in September 1920. Various team members confirmed in testimony to the grand jury that they had received money, either directly from the gamblers or from other team players. By October indictments were handed down to White Sox players who had taken money:

C. Arnold “Chick” Gandil (1st Base)
Eddie Cicotte (Pitcher)
Claude “Lefty” Williams (Pitcher)
Charles “Swede” Risberg (Shortstop)
Oscar “Happy” Felsch (Outfielder)
“Shoeless” Joe Jackson (Outfielder)
Fred McMullin (Infielder)
Buck Weaver (3rd Base)
They would be known forever more as the Black Sox.

Newspapers screamed with headlines of baseball corruption and fans were angry. The American and National Leagues faced a major public relations nightmare fretting that fans would not show up to watch baseball games. They decided to create a baseball commissioner to oversee the game and settled on a sitting federal judge, Kenesaw Mountain Landis, as the man. Known for his directness as a trial judge and a baseball fan, he signed on as the Commissioner of Baseball on 12 November 1920 and was given unprecedented authority to punish players and team owners who did not follow the rules.

Before the trial began in June 1921, the new incoming state attorney for Cook County found the files left by his predecessor in a shambles. Worse, the official grand jury transcript was missing and presumed stolen. This would lead later to an ongoing myth that somehow the signed confessions of the players were missing causing problems at trial. This was not the case at all. The players signed no confessions and only made statements under oath about the bribes they were alleged to have taken. And with shorthand notes of the transcript available, it was reconstructed and used at trial. Also, when Joe Jackson sued the Chicago White Sox, the same transcript was used in that trial as well. 

They would disappear later never to be found, likely because of the court move and the box was simply lost or mislabeled. However, in 1988 a partial copy of legal transcripts was found by the law firm that once employed a White Sox team lawyer. And in 2007 the Chicago History Museum got documents related to the Black Sox Scandal that included documents from both the criminal trial and grand jury (though incomplete) as well from Joe Jackson’s lawsuit. While official documents show certain players retracting their testimony made to the grand jury, there is no proof they ever signed actual confessions. And a monetary award for producing one has been left unclaimed.

The criminal trial began in June 1921 and concluded on August 2. The jury returned in three hours acquitting them all. They all went out to a nice meal at an Italian restaurant that went long into the night with the players believing that they could play baseball. However, the next morning Judge Landis made clear his position:

Regardless of the verdict of juries, no player that throws a ball game; no player that undertakes or promises to throw a ball game; no player that sits in a conference with a bunch of crooked players and gamblers where the ways and means of throwing ball games are planned and discussed and does not promptly tell his club about it, will ever play professional baseball. Of course, I don't know that any of these men will apply for reinstatement, but if they do, the above are at least a few of the rules that will be enforced. Just keep in mind that, regardless of the verdict of juries, baseball is competent to protect itself against crooks, both inside and outside the game.

Landis placed them all on the ineligible list and any contracts they had with the White Sox were terminated. They could not play on any major or minor league team though some– Jackson, Williams, Felsch, and Weaver–played semi-pro baseball. All appeals were rejected. Other players who were found in violation would face similar penalties. Team owners were not exempt either: if a team owner owned or invested in any business where gambling was done, they must sell the business. Landis made sure teams honored their contracts with players and other requirements as well. He closely watched how to major national games–the All-Star Game and World Series–were run and often intervened to implement policies such as how ejections were handled or calling a game too early since the sun was going down. He is severely criticized for keeping blacks out of baseball (they had their own separate league) but it was well known that some clubs would not allow such ballplayers on their teams. It was not until after his death in 1944 and after World War II that the ban would be lifted.

In 2025, Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred made an adjustment to the ineligible policy. He removed 16 deceased players and one deceased owner from the permanent ban list. "Obviously, a person no longer with us cannot represent a threat to the integrity of the game," he wrote to the attorney seeking the ban lifted on the now deceased Pete Rose. He added: “Moreover, it is hard to conceive of a penalty that has more deterrent effect than one that lasts a lifetime with no reprieve.” The list of those with the bans includes all the Chicago Black Sox:

Eddie CicotteBlack Sox Scandal 1921.
Cozy Dolan         New York Giants 1924. As coach he conspired with player Jimmy O’Connell to bribe Philadelphia Phillies player Heiner Sand to throw game between both teams
Phil Douglas      New York Giants 1922. Banned after telling player on St. Louis Browns he planned to spike the pennant race because he hated team manager McGraw.
Happy FelschBlack Sox Scandal 1921.
Chick GandilBlack Sox Scandal 1921.
Joe GedeonBlack Sox Scandal 1921. Played on St. Louis Browns but conspired with gamblers behind the scandal.
Joe JacksonBlack Sox Scandal 1921
Benny KauffNew York Giants 1921. Banned for selling stolen cars.
Fred McMullin  Black Sox Scandal 1921.
Jimmy O'Connell  New York Giants 1924. He and coach Cozy Dolan offered money to Philadelphia Phillies player Heiner Sand to throw game between both teams.
Gene PaulettePhiladelphia Phillies 1921. Banned for associating with gamblers.
Swede RisbergBlack Sox Scandal 1921.
Pete RoseManager Cincinnati Reds 1989. Accepted ban as part of legal settlement for gambling and related issues. Admitted to betting on baseball several years later.
Buck Weaver Black Sox Scandal 1921.
Lefty WilliamsBlack Sox Scandal 1921.

According to current rules, the earliest that these players like Shoeless Joe Jackson or Pete Ross can be eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame is 2028.

The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise dating from the late Spring and Autumn period (roughly 5th century BC). The work, which is attributed to the ancient Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu ("Master Sun"), is composed of 13 chapters. Each one is devoted to a different set of skills or art related to warfare and how it applies to military strategy and tactics. For almost 1,500 years, it was the lead text in an anthology that was formalized as the Seven Military Classics by Emperor Shenzong of Song in 1080. The Art of War remains the most influential strategy text in East Asian warfare,[1] has influenced both East Asian and Western military theory and thinking, and has found a variety of applications in myriad competitive non-military endeavors across the modern world including espionage,[2] culture, politics, business, and sports.[3][4][5][6]

The book contains a detailed explanation and analysis of the 5th-century BC Chinese military, from weapons, environmental conditions, and strategy to rank and discipline. Sun also stressed the importance of intelligence operatives and espionage to the war effort. Considered one of history's finest military tacticians and analysts, his teachings and strategies formed the basis of advanced military training throughout the world.

The book was translated into French and published in 1772 by the French priest Jesuit Jean Joseph Marie Amiot; it was re-published in 1782. A partial translation into English was attempted by British officer Everard Ferguson Calthrop in 1905 under the title The Book of War. The first annotated English translation was completed and published by Lionel Giles in 1910.[7] Military and political leaders such as the Chinese communist revolutionary Mao Zedong, Japanese daimyō Takeda Shingen, Vietnamese general Võ Nguyên Giáp, is cited along with American military generals Douglas MacArthur and Norman Schwarzkopf Jr. as having drawn inspiration from the book.[8]

Outside of military use, The Art of War has also become a source of inspiration in business, politics, sports and esports, and its usage has extended to film and television.

History
Text and commentaries
The Art of War is traditionally attributed to an ancient Chinese military general known as Sun Tzu (pinyin: Sūnzǐ), meaning 'Master Sun'. Sun Tzu is said to have lived in the 6th century BC, but the earliest parts of The Art of War probably date to at least 100 years later.[9]

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, the first of China's 24 dynastic histories, records an early Chinese tradition that a text on military matters was written by one "Sun Wu" (孫武) from the State of Qi, and that this text had been read and studied by King Helü of Wu (r. 514–495 BC).[10] This text was traditionally identified with the received Master Sun's Art of War. The conventional view was that Sun Wu was a military theorist from the end of the Spring and Autumn period (776–471 BC) who fled his home state of Qi to the southeastern Kingdom of Wu, where he is said to have impressed the king with his ability to quickly train even court women in military discipline and to have made Wu's armies powerful enough to challenge their western rivals in the state of Chu. This view is still widely held in China.[11]

The strategist, poet, and warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century AD authored the earliest known commentary to the Art of War.[10] Cao's preface makes clear that he edited the text and removed certain passages, but the extent of his changes were unclear historically.[10] The Art of War appears throughout the bibliographical catalogs of the Chinese dynastic histories, but listings of its divisions and size varied widely.[10]

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

DOCKET DIVE: Did Trapboy Freddy Pay $20,000 Toward Mo3’s Killing?

ATF Task Force Officer Eric Barnes testified that Yella Beezy and Trapboy Freddy made payments for Mo3’s death. But an investigative report Barnes prepared recounts a different account from Theodore Thomas, better known as Jose Bodega: Freddy allegedly never paid his $20,000 share.

Documents obtained by The Docket Diva™ raise questions about the discrepancy, particularly because Trapboy Freddy has not been charged in connection with Mo3’s killing. The apparent lack of a documented payment trail adds another layer to the question of what evidence supports the allegation.

On Friday, October 16, Beezy’s attorneys filed Barnes’ Report of Investigation, along with Bodega’s proffer and sealed grand jury testimony, with the Dallas County Clerk.

Bodega, a longtime friend and associate of Beezy, provided information about Mo3’s killing as part of a federal plea deal.

During Kewon White’s trial in August, Barnes was asked how Beezy and Freddy were connected to the case. He testified:

“They’re the individuals that made payments for Mo3’s death.”

This appears to be the first time Trapboy Freddy was explicitly accused in court of making a payment for Mo3’s killing.

There have been numerous reports over the years suggesting Freddy was connected to the case. Some reports have also stated that he is expected to testify against Beezy in the murder-for-hire trial scheduled to begin this month.

But Barnes’ written report raises questions about that testimony.

According to the report, Bodega told investigators that White killed Mo3 for money that was supposed to come from Beezy, whose legal name is Markies Conway, and Freddy, whose legal name is Devarious Moore.

Bodega alleged that Conway was supposed to pay $20,000, while Freddy was expected to contribute another $20,000.

However, the report states that “Freddy never did.”

According to Bodega’s account, Conway said he would “eat” Freddy’s portion, meaning he would cover the $20,000 Freddy allegedly owed.

The report also says Bodega told investigators that about a week after Mo3’s killing, Jerry Johnson, known as Maserati, told him Conway “had still not paid the rest of the money.”

The report references both a $20,000 and a $40,000 bounty, raising questions about the total amount allegedly promised and how much money was ultimately paid.

Barnes’ testimony characterized both men as having made payments, while his report records Bodega’s claim that Freddy never paid his share and that Conway offered to cover it.

The report summarizes what Bodega allegedly told investigators. It is not a verbatim transcript or an independent determination that the allegations are true.

Yella Beezy’s murder-for-hire trial is scheduled to begin Monday, October 26, in Dallas County, Texas.

White was convicted of Mo3’s murder and sentenced to life in prison.

text:
A Daily Dose of Talmud
Daf Yomi for Everyone, from My Jewish Learning

Bekhorot 32
Read the page on Sefaria
Dr. Sara Ronis
We have learned that a firstborn animal is holy and must be slaughtered and offered on the altar. If that firstborn animal develops a blemish, however, it cannot be sacrificed. Instead, it is given to priests to eat. Either way, the priests end up with the privilege of consuming the bekhor. And while we know that an unblemished firstborn animal can be eaten only by priests because of its sanctity, today’s daf asks:   If the firstborn animal was blemished, can the priests invite non-priestly guests to partake?  The mishnah reports an early rabbinic dispute:   Beit Shammai say: An Israelite cannot be counted with the priest to partake of a blemished firstborn.   And Beit Hillel deem it permitted, and even a gentile.  Predictably, Beit Shammai takes the more stringent stand that only priests can eat this meat. Predictably, Beit Hillel disagrees: Since the firstborn cannot be slaughtered on the altar, the other laws around firstborn animals are relaxed. More surprising, however, is that Beit Hillel permits not only ordinary non-priests to eat the de-sanctified bekhor, but non-Jews as well.The Talmud interrogates each position.    What is the reason of Beit Shammai? As it is written: “But the firstling of cattle, sheep or goats you shall not redeem; they are holy …and their flesh shall be yours, just like the wave breast and the right thigh, it shall be yours” (Numbers 18:17–18). Just as there (with regard to the breast and the thigh) priests may partake of it but an Israelite may not, so too here (the blemished firstborn) only priests may partake of it, but an Israelite may not.   Numbers 18:18 compares the firstborn animal to the priestly gifts of breast and thigh meat. Beit Shammai reads this comparison, reasonably, as indicating the same populations can legally eat each meat. If the breast and thigh must be “yours” (God is speaking to Aaron and his sons in this verse), then the firstborn animal must also belong exclusively to priests.   The Talmud’s analysis of Beit Shammai’s position doesn’t note that these biblical verses are explicitly about an unblemished firstborn animal in the time of the Temple. Apparently, if Deuteronomy doesn’t distinguish between a blemished and an unblemished firstborn here, neither does Beit Shammai. At the top of tomorrow’s daf, however, the Talmud will insist that Beit Hillel identified this very weakness in Beit Shammai’s argument.   And Beit Hillel: This statement applies only to an unblemished firstborn offering! But concerning a blemished firstborn it is written: “You shall eat it within your gates; the impure and the pure may eat it alike” (Deuteronomy 12:22; see Deuteronomy 15:22). And if a ritually impure priest, who may not eat the meat of offerings of lesser sanctity, may eat the meat of a blemished firstborn, then a non-priest, who may eat the meat of offerings of lesser sanctity, is it not logical that he may eat the meat of a blemished firstborn offering?   Beit Hillel uses a kal va’chomer (a fortiori) argument: A non-priest is permitted to eat offerings of lesser sanctity that a ritually impure priest cannot eat. So if a ritually impure priest is permitted to eat a blemished firstborn, shouldn't a non-priest be allowed to eat it as well?  In this case, as in almost all cases, the halakhah follows Beit Hillel. This, in turn, likely had profound social effects. Beit Hillel is more expansive regarding who can eat the meat, yet still insists that the animal retains a special status. The blemished firstborn animal thus creates an opportunity for those with more social power to invite others to join them at their table, whether or not the guests are themselves Jewish.

Dismissing Yeshua as "one of 50 failed claimants" ignores the explicit prophetic constraints of the Tanakh and documented history:

1. The Second Temple Constraint (Daniel 9:24–26, Haggai 2:7–9, Malachi 3:1):

The Hebrew Scriptures explicitly placed the arrival of the Messiah before the destruction of the Second Temple. Daniel 9 specified that the Mashiach would be cut off prior to the destruction of the city and the sanctuary (70 CE). With the Temple destroyed, the sacrificial system ended, and the genealogical records obliterated, no claimant arising after 70 CE can ever meet the canonical requirements of the Tanakh.

2. The Incomparable Outcome:

The other Second Temple figures (Theudas, Judas the Galilean, Bar Kokhba) led failed militaristic insurrections; their deaths extinguished their movements. Yeshua was crucified, an empty tomb was proclaimed in the very city of His execution, and His disciples—witnesses of His resurrection—transformed the ancient world. Through Him alone, the pagan nations turned from idols to worship the God of Israel, fulfilling Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6 ("a light to the nations"). No other claimant in Jewish history did that.

3. Sovereign Authority vs. Rabbinic Borrowing:

Hillel and Shammai cited predecessor traditions ("Rabbi A said in the name of Rabbi B"). Yeshua spoke with unmediated divine authority: "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you" (Matthew 7:28–29). Neither Hillel nor Shammai claimed to forgive sins, possess authority over the Sabbath, or offer their life as an atonement for the sins of the world (Isaiah 53).

4. The Indictment of Unbelief (Deuteronomy 18:18–19):

To reduce the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets to a derivative mashup of Hillel, Shammai, and the Essenes elevates human schools of thought above the Living God. God warned through Moses: "I will raise up for them a Prophet like you from among their brethren, and will put My words in His mouth... and whoever will not hear My words which He speaks in My name, I will require it of him." (Deut 18:18–19). Treating the Messiah's arrival with casual apathy does not demonstrate intellectual detachment; it demonstrates the very spiritual blindness the prophets lamented (Isaiah 6:9–10).

Comparing the One who fulfilled the prophetic timeline of the Hebrew prophets to 7th-century Arabia is a deflection. The question is not about pagan religions; it is about whether you believe what Moses, Isaiah, and Daniel actually wrote concerning the timing, the sacrifice, and the identity of Israel's Messiah.

To shrug off the explicit timeline of Daniel, the blood-atonement of Isaiah 53, and the destruction of the Second Temple as "unremarkable" is not enlightened skepticism; it is a fatal spiritual gamble. Scripture issues a severe warning to those who casually dismiss the testimony of the prophets: "Beware therefore, lest what has been spoken in the prophets come upon you: 'Behold, you despisers, marvel and perish! For I work a work in your days, a work which you will by no means believe, though one were to declare it to you'" (Acts 13:40–41; Habakkuk 1:5). The sovereign God of Abraham will not accept human indifference as a defense when He holds every soul accountable to the Word He declared through His prophets. The ledger of the Tanakh is closed, its demands are absolute, and you stand without an altar, without a temple, and without an atonement outside of the One whom the Scriptures foretold.

text:
I was reading Psalms today and noticed something familiar. AI helped me make the connection real and I am really excited and want to share:

Psalm 141:2 is a remarkable Old Testament anticipation of what Revelation later makes explicit. The psalmist petitions God: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice!” This prayer expresses the exact theological reality that John’s apocalyptic vision would later unveil: that prayers themselves function as precious offerings ascending before God’s throne.

What makes this connection so striking is the temporal arc. The psalmist is speaking *prophetically* about prayer’s true nature, requesting that God regard his words and gestures with the same sacred weight as the temple’s formal ritual offerings. In Luke’s account of Zechariah’s priestly service, the people were praying outside the temple “at the hour of incense,” (Luke 1:8–10) showing that this connection between prayer and incense was embedded in Jewish worship practice. Yet Psalm 141 goes further, asking God to *transform* prayer itself into incense, to treat the worshiper’s words as if they were the fragrant offering burning on the altar.

Centuries later, John receives the vision that confirms this request has been answered. The elders hold “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints,” (Rev 5:8) and the angel offers incense “with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,” with “the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God.” The psalmist’s plea becomes reality in the heavenly throne room.

This progression reveals how Scripture unfolds: the Old Testament saint prays for what the New Testament saint discovers has always been true.

text:
Have you felt separated from God by the barriers of sin and division.

Do the conflicts around you mirror the ancient walls that kept people apart.

What would it mean if those walls were destroyed to create one new humanity.

Dive into the reconciliation through Christ from Ephesians 2:12-22 where Gentiles and Jews are joined into a holy temple built on the cornerstone.

Embracing Belonging in Gods Family Ephesians 2

In the reading from Ephesians we find a powerful message about how Christ unites people from all backgrounds. This passage from the letter to the Ephesians invites us to reflect on our identity as part of a larger community. It speaks to those who feel on the outside and reassures them of their place within the household of God. Through Christs sacrifice barriers are removed allowing for true reconciliation. This offers hope to anyone striving to live faithfully even when challenges arise in daily life.

What Walls Does Christ Tear Down in Our Lives?

The early verses of this reading describe a time when some felt far off and separated from the promises of God. Christ comes to bridge that gap by his blood bringing people close who once stood at a distance. This act of love reminds us that no matter how disconnected we might feel at times our efforts to seek goodness are met with open arms. The message encourages those who try their best yet stumble knowing that peace is available through faith. It paints a picture of unity where former divisions fade away in the light of shared purpose.

How Can We Become Fellow Citizens with the Holy Ones?

You are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of the household of God. This beautiful quote highlights the shift from isolation to inclusion in a divine family that welcomes all who turn toward it. It reassures readers that their place is secure not because of perfection but through the grace that builds us up together. For those working to live out their faith amid imperfections this serves as a gentle reminder that belonging comes from Christ rather than personal achievement alone. The idea fosters a sense of companionship with others on the same journey making the spiritual path feel less lonely and more supported.

Building on the Foundation of Apostles and Prophets

The passage continues by describing how the community rests on the solid base laid by apostles and prophets with Christ as the key stone. This foundation provides stability for anyone seeking to grow in their spiritual life even during seasons of doubt or setback. It shows that our individual contributions join with those of the past to create something enduring and beautiful. People trying to do good can draw strength from this image knowing their small steps add to a greater whole guided by divine wisdom. The reading thus inspires perseverance with an uplifting view of ongoing construction in faith.

Why Is Christ the Cornerstone for Our Faith Journey?

Finally the text explains that in Christ the whole structure grows into a holy temple where God dwells. This vision lifts up the idea that we are not alone but part of a living edifice filled with presence and purpose. It encourages daily attempts at kindness and prayer by showing how they fit into something eternal and supportive. Even when progress feels slow the assurance remains that growth happens through connection to this cornerstone. The overall message leaves readers with a sense of hope and belonging that sustains them forward.

May the peace of Christ be with you,

🙏 @RCatholicPrayer

text:
Nearly 50 years after a young couple vanished in the Grand Canyon, a skeleton with a bullet in the skull turned up hidden in a canoe.

It was at the home of one of the last people to see them alive.

In the fall of 1928, Glen and Bessie Hyde set off down the Colorado River in a boat they'd built themselves. They had married that April. He was 27. She was 18 and had never been on a river. Glen wanted a speed record through the Grand Canyon, and they carried no life jackets.

At Green River, Utah, a veteran river man took one look at the boat and thought it looked like a coffin. They reached the heart of the canyon in 26 days anyway, a record.

Before the most dangerous stretch, they stopped to see photographer Emery Kolb. Bessie was worn out. Kolb urged them to spend the winter with him and wait. He even offered them his life jackets. Glen turned it all down. Two days later, they vanished.

Army pilots spotted their boat at Diamond Creek, undamaged, with everything still on board: clothes, food, Glen's rifle, a camera with film, Bessie's journal. Their bodies were never found.

Nearly 50 years later, after Kolb died, a skeleton turned up hidden in a canoe in a shed at his home, with a bullet in the skull. An old rumor came back: that Kolb had killed Glen to win Bessie. But when a forensic anthropologist laid a photo of Glen over the skull, the eye sockets, cheekbones and chin didn't match. Later studies found the bones belonged to a man no older than 22 who died no earlier than 1932.

Then there's 1971. People on a river trip said an older woman camping with them at Diamond Creek, where the boat was found, claimed she was Bessie Hyde and had killed her husband after a fight. Tracked down years later in Ohio, she denied all of it.

No trace of Glen or Bessie Hyde has ever been found.

What do you think happened to them?

📂 Case file: The Disappearance of Glen and Bessie Hyde (Grand Canyon, 1928)

text:
DEMOCRACY DOCKET:
Exclusive: Thousands of North Carolina ballots set to be rejected after GOP imposed strict new rules, data shows

Data shared exclusively with Democracy Docket offers an unusually stark example of how Republican-backed voting restrictions, especially those targeting mail ballots, can directly cause large numbers of eligible voters to be disenfranchised.

Some Democratic strongholds are seeing mail ballot rejection rates as high as 7% to 8%, the data shows.

The state imposed the ballot rules — championed by the GOP — which established new signature matching and envelope sealing requirements, on the same day mail voting began. A federal judge this week ruled that they will remain in effect for the midterms.

One of the biggest obstacles facing scrutiny is a new requirement for voters to put their ballot inside and seal an inner envelope, which then gets put into an outer envelope. This appears to be leading to inner envelopes being left unsealed, causing higher rates of rejections, advocates say.

If that wasn’t enough, the judge who approved the restrictive new measures also upheld a strict GOP-led voter ID law ten years ago that an appeals court later found targeted Black voters “with almost surgical precision.”
